- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review changed code for reuse, quality, and efficiency, then fix any issues found.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled remote agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring remote agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Build, debug, and optimize Claude API / Anthropic SDK apps. Apps built with this skill should include prompt caching. Also handles migrating existing Claude API code between Claude model versions (4.5 → 4.6, 4.6 → 4.7, retired-model replacements).

SKIP: file imports `openai`/other-provider SDK, filename like `*-openai.py`/`*-generic.py`, provider-neutral code, general programming/ML.

- review: Review a pull request
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

SprintHub — Technical Specification
v2
Cahier des charges · Feature roadmap and improvement backlog
May 2026

SprintHub — Technical Specification
v2
Document type: Cahier des charges
Version: 2.0
Date: May 2026
Status: Draft — for planning purposes

Context
SprintHub v1.0 shipped with a full GitHub Projects v2 integration: board view, PR
dashboard, CI status, standup generator, conflict detection, CODEOWNERS hints,
merge button, and metadata editing. This document defines the next iteration.
The findings below come from a systematic audit of the v1 codebase, analysing
every fetched data field, every message type, every component, and every API call
to identify what is underused, what is missing, and where the experience has
friction.

Part 1 — Quick Wins
Items that can be implemented in under a day each. High ROI, low risk.

1.1 Stale item badges on board cards
Problem: The stale quality flag (> 7 days without activity) is computed in
DetailPanel but only visible after clicking a card to open the side panel. In the
main board and LaunchpadView, stale cards are visually identical to active ones.

 Solution: Compute the stale flag in ColumnGroup and LaunchpadView rows
directly from the updatedAt field (already present on every BoardItem). Render a
small amber dot or “7d+” tag on the card.
Config: Expose the threshold as a setting sprinthub.staleThresholdDays
(default: 7).

1.2 Quality flags on board cards
Problem: computeQualityFlags in DetailPanel produces useful signals — large
PR, no description, no tests, no reviewers — but these are invisible in the card/list
view. A reviewer has to open the panel to discover that a PR has 1 400 changed lines
or no description.
Solution: Run the same logic at the card level. Show 1–2 of the most severe flags as
compact chips on the card bottom row. Limit to 2 chips to avoid cluttering small
cards.

1.3 Keyboard shortcuts
Problem: Every interaction in SprintHub requires a mouse click. Power users
working through a sprint review or standup will lose time to the trackpad.
Shortcuts to implement:
Key

Action

Cmd/Ctrl + K

Focus the search input
Close the detail panel
Trigger a manual refresh
Navigate items in the active view
Open selected item in detail panel

Esc
R
↑ / ↓
Enter

Implementation: keydown listener on the webview root, dispatching state updates
via React.

1.4 Persist sprint filter across tab switches
Problem: Selecting “Sprint 157” then switching from Dashboard to Pull Requests
tab resets the sprint filter. The user has to re-select it every time.
Solution: Store sprintFilter in vscodeApi.getState() /
vscodeApi.setState(). Restore on mount. This also survives panel closes and
reopens.

 1.5 Remember last-used merge method
Problem: The merge dropdown in the detail panel (MergeButton) always defaults
to “Squash and merge”. Teams typically use the same method every time.
Solution: Persist the last-used merge method in vscode.workspace.state (or the
webview state). Pre-select it on next open.

1.6 API rate limit display
Problem: There is no visibility into GitHub API quota consumption. When the
status bar shows stale data or fetches fail silently, the user has no way to know if rate
limiting is the cause.
Solution: After each GraphQL/REST call, read the X-RateLimit-Remaining and
X-RateLimit-Reset headers (available on REST responses; GraphQL exposes
rateLimit in the response body). Display in the footer as “API 45/60” with a
tooltip showing the reset time. Color it amber below 20, red below 5.

1.7 Issue body caching
Problem: fetchBody is called on demand each time a detail panel opens. The same
issue body is re-fetched every time the user opens and closes a card.
Solution: Add an itemBodyCache: Map<string, string> in App.tsx (keyed by
itemId). On itemBody message, populate the cache. On subsequent opens of the
same item, skip the fetch if the cache entry exists.

1.8 Repo labels preloading
Problem: The first time the label editor opens for any issue, it triggers a
fetchRepoLabels network request. The user sees “Loading…” and has to wait.
Solution: After the initial board load, batch-fetch labels for all unique repositories
visible on the board. One GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/labels call per repo,
parallelised. Populate repoLabelsCache proactively so the editor opens instantly.

Part 2 — UX Improvements
Interactions that currently require too many steps or produce confusing results.

 2.1 Pin detail panel while browsing
Problem: When the detail panel is open, clicking another card replaces its content.
Users who want to compare two items, or who want to reference one PR’s
description while looking at the board, have no way to keep a panel open.
Solution: Add a pin icon (📌) to the detail panel header. When pinned, clicking a
board card opens a second panel or highlights the new item without replacing the
current one. Alternatively, a simpler approach: “Open in new tab” that opens the PR
URL in the browser while keeping the panel.

2.2 Inline “Assign to Me” action
Problem: Assigning yourself to a PR or issue currently requires: open detail panel
→ scroll to metadata editor → fetch repo labels → add assignee. Four interactions
minimum.
Solution: Add a small “Assign me” button directly on the card’s assignee area when
viewerLogin is known and the user is not already an assignee. Clicking it calls
PATCH /repos/{owner}/{repo}/issues/{number} with assignees:
[viewerLogin] and updates the card optimistically.

2.3 Detail panel updates on board refresh
Problem: If a PR is open in the detail panel and merges externally (via GitHub web
or another team member), the panel continues to show OPEN. The next board refresh
updates the card in the list, but the panel is not notified.
Solution: When a data message arrives with a refreshed board, find the currently
open detailItem by ID, replace it with the updated version from the payload if
found, and re-render the panel.

2.4 Empty state improvements
Problem: When the sprint filter is set and the current view has no results, the UI
shows a generic “No open pull requests found” message. The user does not know if
the filter is to blame.
Solution: Detect when the board has items but the current filter combination
produces zero results. Show a contextual message: “No PRs in Sprint 157. Try
clearing the sprint filter or switching tabs.” with a one-click “Clear filter” button.

2.5 Conflict threat visibility in detail panel
Problem: conflictThreats state exists in App.tsx and the banner is shown at the
top of the main view, but the detail panel for an individual PR does not show which
of its files are in conflict.

 Solution: When the detail panel is open for a PR, cross-reference
conflictThreats with prFiles to highlight conflicting files with an amber
warning icon in the PRFilesSection. Show the conflicting PR number as a tooltip.

Part 3 — New Features
Substantial additions that require new API calls or new UI surfaces.

3.1 Review queue tab
What: A dedicated tab showing every PR across all board repos that the current user
has been requested to review, sorted by waiting time.
Why: The “Assigned to me” filter in the Dashboard only shows PRs you authored
or are assigned to. Requested reviews are not surfaced in a dedicated view and can
be missed.
Data: reviewRequests field is already fetched on every BoardItem. Filter items
where reviewRequests.some(r => r.login === viewerLogin).
UI: New 'review-queue' tab in the toolbar. Same row layout as LaunchpadView.
Sort by updatedAt ascending (oldest first). Show “Waiting X days” badge.

3.2 Milestone progress visualization
What: Add a visual progress bar to each milestone in the Milestones tab showing
the percentage of issues/PRs that are closed or merged.
Why: The current Milestones tab lists items by milestone but gives no signal about
how close a milestone is to completion. Users have to count manually.
Data: state field is present on every BoardItem. Group by milestone, compute
closedCount / totalCount.
UI: Progress bar component below each milestone header. Show “12 / 20 closed ·
due Jun 15” inline. Color: green above 80%, amber 40–80%, red below 40% with
less than 14 days to dueOn.
Config: No additional API calls needed — all data is already loaded.

3.3 PR activity feed
What: A chronological feed of recent PR/issue activity (merges, reviews submitted,
new comments, state changes) across all board repos.
Why: The board shows current state but not what changed recently. After a weekend
or a day off, there is no quick way to catch up.

 Data: GitHub Search API, already used in the standup generator
(generateStandupMarkdown). Extend the query window to 72h and include more
event types.
UI: New 'activity' tab. Timeline layout: avatar + action + PR title + timestamp.
Group by day. Lazy-load older entries.

3.4 Reviewer suggestions from CODEOWNERS
What: When viewing a PR with no reviewers assigned, suggest reviewers based on
the CODEOWNERS file for the changed files.
Why: CODEOWNERS data is already fetched and displayed per file
(fetchCodeowners in githubService.ts, resolveCodeowners in
DetailPanel). The logical next step is to close the loop: use that data to suggest or
auto-assign reviewers.
UI: “Suggest reviewers” button in the detail panel header (only shown when
reviewRequests is empty and codeownersEntries is loaded). Opens a dropdown
listing the CODEOWNERS matched from the changed files. Clicking one calls
POST /repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls/{number}/requested_reviewers.

3.5 Offline fallback / last-known state
What: Cache the last successfully loaded board state in
vscode.workspace.state. On startup or when the API is unreachable, show the
cached data with a “Last synced X ago” banner instead of a blank error state.
Why: Network blips, VPN changes, and GitHub outages cause SprintHub to go
blank. The data from 10 minutes ago is still useful.
Implementation: - After every successful data message, serialize RunwayData to
context.workspaceState.update('sprinthub.lastData', payload). - On
startup, load from workspaceState while the first fetch is in-flight. - Show a nonblocking last synced X ago badge in the footer instead of blocking on load.

3.6 Sprint velocity and burndown
What: A simple burndown chart for the active sprint: issues opened vs. closed per
day over the sprint duration.
Why: Teams running Scrum need to know if they are on track mid-sprint. Currently
SprintHub shows a static snapshot with no trend.
Data: Sprint start/end dates are derivable from the iteration field (sprint +
sprintField on BoardItem). Issue state and updatedAt give close dates. A REST
call to GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/issues?
state=closed&since={sprintStart} fills the gaps.

 UI: Small sparkline chart in the Dashboard toolbar when a sprint filter is active. No
full chart library needed — pure SVG path from computed data points.
Config: Optional. Hidden unless sprint filter is active.

3.7 GitHub Notifications badge
What: Fetch unread GitHub notifications count and display it as a badge on the
SprintHub activity bar icon.
Why: Notifications (mentions, review requests, CI failures on your PRs) are
currently only visible in the browser. A badge would make SprintHub the single
place to check.
Data: GET /notifications REST API. Returns unread count and type (mention,
review_request, ci_activity, etc.).
Implementation: Poll every refreshInterval minutes alongside the board
refresh. Use vscode.window.createStatusBarItem or the existing status bar
item for display. Badge via VS Code’s setBadge API on the webview panel.

3.8 Custom column aliases
What: Allow teams to map their custom column names to SprintHub’s standard
grouping logic.
Why: The grouping in LaunchpadView (getPRGroup) checks
item.column?.toLowerCase() === 'ready for review' hardcoded. Teams

using “In Review”, “Awaiting QA”, or other names get incorrect grouping.
Solution: Add a sprinthub.columnAliases setting (JSON object): { "ready
for review": ["In Review", "Awaiting Review", "PR Review"] }. The
grouping function reads this map before falling back to the default.

Part 4 — Performance
4.1 Debounced search
The filteredGroups memo in App.tsx runs on every keystroke scanning all
items. For large boards (100+ items), this is wasteful.
Fix: Debounce the search input by 150ms. Add a simple useDebounce hook (no
external dependency needed — 5 lines of code).

 4.2 Avoid config reload on cosmetic changes
SprintHubPanel calls _loadData() on every config update, including changes to
liquidGlass, theme, and colorBlind. These settings are purely cosmetic and do

not affect API calls.
Fix: In _sendConfig, compare the new config against the stored _lastConfig.
Only call _loadData() if a data-relevant field (owner, projectNumber,
ownerType, statusFieldName, refreshInterval) changed.

4.3 CODEOWNERS regex memoization
matchesCodeownersPattern compiles a RegExp on every call. For a PR with 30

changed files and a CODEOWNERS with 50 patterns, this is 1 500 regex
compilations per render.
Fix: Memoize entries.map(e => ({ ...e, re:
compilePattern(e.pattern) })) in PRFilesSection via useMemo, keyed on
codeownersEntries.

4.4 Virtualized list for large boards
For projects with 200+ items, rendering all cards simultaneously causes jank. The
content div scrolls but all DOM nodes are mounted.
Fix: Implement a simple windowed list using IntersectionObserver — render
placeholder divs of fixed height for off-screen items, replace with real cards as they
enter the viewport. No external library needed.

Part 6 — Error Handling Gaps
6.1 Inaccessible repository warning
When fetchLinkedPRsFromRepos receives a 403, it silently skips the repo. The
user never knows that data from a restricted repo is missing.
Fix: Collect skipped repos during fetch. If any were skipped, show a dismissible
warning: “Could not load data from: repo-name (permission denied).”

6.2 Partial load recovery
If pagination fails mid-load (cursor-based, 100 items per page), the whole load fails.
For boards with 200+ items, this loses all data.
Fix: Implement partial load recovery — keep the items fetched so far, show a
warning banner “Loaded 100 / 240 items — refresh to retry.”

 6.3 Stale detail panel on external merge
If the user is viewing a PR detail panel and that PR merges externally, the panel
continues to show OPEN. The state is stale.
Fix: On every data board refresh, find the currently open detailItem by id and
replace it with the updated payload version. This is a one-line change in the data
message handler.

Part 7 — UI / Visual Overhaul
Design-level improvements identified in the first round of user testing. These affect
the visual layer and the settings UX without changing data fetching logic.

7.1 Smart org and project picker in settings
Problem: The settings modal currently requires users to type the exact organization
login and project number from memory. Both values require leaving VS Code to
look up in a browser.
Solution: - On settings modal open, fire GET /user/orgs to retrieve all
organizations the authenticated user belongs to. - Render the owner field as a
combobox backed by a <datalist> populated with fetched org logins. Supports
keyboard autocomplete and manual entry. - When the owner field has a valid value
(on blur or after a 700 ms debounce), fire a GraphQL query for
organization(login).projectsV2(first: 20) (or
user(login).projectsV2) and populate a <select> dropdown for the project
number field, showing each project as #N — Title. - Fall back to the plain number
input if the fetch fails or returns an empty list.
New message types: - { type: 'fetchOrgs' } — webview → extension { type: 'fetchProjectsList'; owner: string; ownerType:
'organization' | 'user' } — webview → extension { type: 'orgsList'; logins: string[]; viewerLogin: string } —
extension → webview - { type: 'projectsList'; owner: string;
projects: Array<{ number: number; title: string }> } — extension →

webview
Additional UX: When ownerType is user, auto-populate the owner field with the
authenticated viewerLogin. Expose a theme (dark / light) toggle now that the light
theme is polished.

7.2 Liquid Glass as the sole visual mode
Problem: The UI ships two parallel style systems — a flat “default” mode and the
liquid glass overlay. This doubles CSS surface area and complicates every future
design change. The flat mode is visually less interesting and no longer the intended
experience.

 Solution: - Always apply the liquid-glass CSS class regardless of the config
setting. - Remove the Liquid Glass toggle from the settings modal. - Archive the flat
style rules (the base card/panel backgrounds) — they are superseded by the glass
layer. - Keep the sprinthub.liquidGlass config key for backwards compatibility
but ignore its value at runtime.
Impact: All new UI components and CSS additions are written only for the glass
context.

7.3 Liquid Glass light theme
Problem: The light theme exists in the codebase (body.light-theme) but is
commented out in the settings panel. When enabled manually, it renders flat
Catppuccin Latte colours without any glass effect — the two systems are not
combined.

overrides both the dark glass backgrounds and the flat light backgrounds:

7.4 Liquid Glass visual enhancements (dark mode)
Problem: The current glass effect is functional but its depth and refractive quality
can be pushed further.
Improvements: 1. Background depth — Replace the single radial-gradient

3. Group header shimmer — Add a subtle @keyframes shimmer on the ::before

SprintHub — Technical Specification
v2
Document type: Cahier des charges
Version: 2.0
Date: May 2026
Status: Draft — for planning purposes

Context
SprintHub v1.0 shipped with a full GitHub Projects v2 integration: board view, PR
dashboard, CI status, standup generator, conflict detection, CODEOWNERS hints,
merge button, and metadata editing. This document defines the next iteration.
The findings below come from a systematic audit of the v1 codebase, analysing
every fetched data field, every message type, every component, and every API call
to identify what is underused, what is missing, and where the experience has
friction.

Part 1 — Quick Wins
Items that can be implemented in under a day each. High ROI, low risk.

1.1 Stale item badges on board cards
Problem: The stale quality flag (> 7 days without activity) is computed in
DetailPanel but only visible after clicking a card to open the side panel. In the
main board and LaunchpadView, stale cards are visually identical to active ones.

 Solution: Compute the stale flag in ColumnGroup and LaunchpadView rows
directly from the updatedAt field (already present on every BoardItem). Render a
small amber dot or “7d+” tag on the card.
Config: Expose the threshold as a setting sprinthub.staleThresholdDays
(default: 7).

1.2 Quality flags on board cards
Problem: computeQualityFlags in DetailPanel produces useful signals — large
PR, no description, no tests, no reviewers — but these are invisible in the card/list
view. A reviewer has to open the panel to discover that a PR has 1 400 changed lines
or no description.
Solution: Run the same logic at the card level. Show 1–2 of the most severe flags as
compact chips on the card bottom row. Limit to 2 chips to avoid cluttering small
cards.

1.3 Keyboard shortcuts
Problem: Every interaction in SprintHub requires a mouse click. Power users
working through a sprint review or standup will lose time to the trackpad.
Shortcuts to implement:
Key

Action

Cmd/Ctrl + K

Focus the search input
Close the detail panel
Trigger a manual refresh
Navigate items in the active view
Open selected item in detail panel

Esc
R
↑ / ↓
Enter

Implementation: keydown listener on the webview root, dispatching state updates
via React.

1.4 Persist sprint filter across tab switches
Problem: Selecting “Sprint 157” then switching from Dashboard to Pull Requests
tab resets the sprint filter. The user has to re-select it every time.
Solution: Store sprintFilter in vscodeApi.getState() /
vscodeApi.setState(). Restore on mount. This also survives panel closes and
reopens.

 1.5 Remember last-used merge method
Problem: The merge dropdown in the detail panel (MergeButton) always defaults
to “Squash and merge”. Teams typically use the same method every time.
Solution: Persist the last-used merge method in vscode.workspace.state (or the
webview state). Pre-select it on next open.

1.6 API rate limit display
Problem: There is no visibility into GitHub API quota consumption. When the
status bar shows stale data or fetches fail silently, the user has no way to know if rate
limiting is the cause.
Solution: After each GraphQL/REST call, read the X-RateLimit-Remaining and
X-RateLimit-Reset headers (available on REST responses; GraphQL exposes
rateLimit in the response body). Display in the footer as “API 45/60” with a
tooltip showing the reset time. Color it amber below 20, red below 5.

1.7 Issue body caching
Problem: fetchBody is called on demand each time a detail panel opens. The same
issue body is re-fetched every time the user opens and closes a card.
Solution: Add an itemBodyCache: Map<string, string> in App.tsx (keyed by
itemId). On itemBody message, populate the cache. On subsequent opens of the
same item, skip the fetch if the cache entry exists.

1.8 Repo labels preloading
Problem: The first time the label editor opens for any issue, it triggers a
fetchRepoLabels network request. The user sees “Loading…” and has to wait.
Solution: After the initial board load, batch-fetch labels for all unique repositories
visible on the board. One GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/labels call per repo,
parallelised. Populate repoLabelsCache proactively so the editor opens instantly.

Part 2 — UX Improvements
Interactions that currently require too many steps or produce confusing results.

 2.1 Pin detail panel while browsing
Problem: When the detail panel is open, clicking another card replaces its content.
Users who want to compare two items, or who want to reference one PR’s
description while looking at the board, have no way to keep a panel open.
Solution: Add a pin icon (📌) to the detail panel header. When pinned, clicking a
board card opens a second panel or highlights the new item without replacing the
current one. Alternatively, a simpler approach: “Open in new tab” that opens the PR
URL in the browser while keeping the panel.

2.2 Inline “Assign to Me” action
Problem: Assigning yourself to a PR or issue currently requires: open detail panel
→ scroll to metadata editor → fetch repo labels → add assignee. Four interactions
minimum.
Solution: Add a small “Assign me” button directly on the card’s assignee area when
viewerLogin is known and the user is not already an assignee. Clicking it calls
PATCH /repos/{owner}/{repo}/issues/{number} with assignees:
[viewerLogin] and updates the card optimistically.

2.3 Detail panel updates on board refresh
Problem: If a PR is open in the detail panel and merges externally (via GitHub web
or another team member), the panel continues to show OPEN. The next board refresh
updates the card in the list, but the panel is not notified.
Solution: When a data message arrives with a refreshed board, find the currently
open detailItem by ID, replace it with the updated version from the payload if
found, and re-render the panel.

2.4 Empty state improvements
Problem: When the sprint filter is set and the current view has no results, the UI
shows a generic “No open pull requests found” message. The user does not know if
the filter is to blame.
Solution: Detect when the board has items but the current filter combination
produces zero results. Show a contextual message: “No PRs in Sprint 157. Try
clearing the sprint filter or switching tabs.” with a one-click “Clear filter” button.

2.5 Conflict threat visibility in detail panel
Problem: conflictThreats state exists in App.tsx and the banner is shown at the
top of the main view, but the detail panel for an individual PR does not show which
of its files are in conflict.

 Solution: When the detail panel is open for a PR, cross-reference
conflictThreats with prFiles to highlight conflicting files with an amber
warning icon in the PRFilesSection. Show the conflicting PR number as a tooltip.

Part 3 — New Features
Substantial additions that require new API calls or new UI surfaces.

3.1 Review queue tab
What: A dedicated tab showing every PR across all board repos that the current user
has been requested to review, sorted by waiting time.
Why: The “Assigned to me” filter in the Dashboard only shows PRs you authored
or are assigned to. Requested reviews are not surfaced in a dedicated view and can
be missed.
Data: reviewRequests field is already fetched on every BoardItem. Filter items
where reviewRequests.some(r => r.login === viewerLogin).
UI: New 'review-queue' tab in the toolbar. Same row layout as LaunchpadView.
Sort by updatedAt ascending (oldest first). Show “Waiting X days” badge.

3.2 Milestone progress visualization
What: Add a visual progress bar to each milestone in the Milestones tab showing
the percentage of issues/PRs that are closed or merged.
Why: The current Milestones tab lists items by milestone but gives no signal about
how close a milestone is to completion. Users have to count manually.
Data: state field is present on every BoardItem. Group by milestone, compute
closedCount / totalCount.
UI: Progress bar component below each milestone header. Show “12 / 20 closed ·
due Jun 15” inline. Color: green above 80%, amber 40–80%, red below 40% with
less than 14 days to dueOn.
Config: No additional API calls needed — all data is already loaded.

3.3 PR activity feed
What: A chronological feed of recent PR/issue activity (merges, reviews submitted,
new comments, state changes) across all board repos.
Why: The board shows current state but not what changed recently. After a weekend
or a day off, there is no quick way to catch up.

 Data: GitHub Search API, already used in the standup generator
(generateStandupMarkdown). Extend the query window to 72h and include more
event types.
UI: New 'activity' tab. Timeline layout: avatar + action + PR title + timestamp.
Group by day. Lazy-load older entries.

3.4 Reviewer suggestions from CODEOWNERS
What: When viewing a PR with no reviewers assigned, suggest reviewers based on
the CODEOWNERS file for the changed files.
Why: CODEOWNERS data is already fetched and displayed per file
(fetchCodeowners in githubService.ts, resolveCodeowners in
DetailPanel). The logical next step is to close the loop: use that data to suggest or
auto-assign reviewers.
UI: “Suggest reviewers” button in the detail panel header (only shown when
reviewRequests is empty and codeownersEntries is loaded). Opens a dropdown
listing the CODEOWNERS matched from the changed files. Clicking one calls
POST /repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls/{number}/requested_reviewers.

3.5 Offline fallback / last-known state
What: Cache the last successfully loaded board state in
vscode.workspace.state. On startup or when the API is unreachable, show the
cached data with a “Last synced X ago” banner instead of a blank error state.
Why: Network blips, VPN changes, and GitHub outages cause SprintHub to go
blank. The data from 10 minutes ago is still useful.
Implementation: - After every successful data message, serialize RunwayData to
context.workspaceState.update('sprinthub.lastData', payload). - On
startup, load from workspaceState while the first fetch is in-flight. - Show a nonblocking last synced X ago badge in the footer instead of blocking on load.

3.6 Sprint velocity and burndown
What: A simple burndown chart for the active sprint: issues opened vs. closed per
day over the sprint duration.
Why: Teams running Scrum need to know if they are on track mid-sprint. Currently
SprintHub shows a static snapshot with no trend.
Data: Sprint start/end dates are derivable from the iteration field (sprint +
sprintField on BoardItem). Issue state and updatedAt give close dates. A REST
call to GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/issues?
state=closed&since={sprintStart} fills the gaps.

 UI: Small sparkline chart in the Dashboard toolbar when a sprint filter is active. No
full chart library needed — pure SVG path from computed data points.
Config: Optional. Hidden unless sprint filter is active.

3.7 GitHub Notifications badge
What: Fetch unread GitHub notifications count and display it as a badge on the
SprintHub activity bar icon.
Why: Notifications (mentions, review requests, CI failures on your PRs) are
currently only visible in the browser. A badge would make SprintHub the single
place to check.
Data: GET /notifications REST API. Returns unread count and type (mention,
review_request, ci_activity, etc.).
Implementation: Poll every refreshInterval minutes alongside the board
refresh. Use vscode.window.createStatusBarItem or the existing status bar
item for display. Badge via VS Code’s setBadge API on the webview panel.

3.8 Custom column aliases
What: Allow teams to map their custom column names to SprintHub’s standard
grouping logic.
Why: The grouping in LaunchpadView (getPRGroup) checks
item.column?.toLowerCase() === 'ready for review' hardcoded. Teams

using “In Review”, “Awaiting QA”, or other names get incorrect grouping.
Solution: Add a sprinthub.columnAliases setting (JSON object): { "ready
for review": ["In Review", "Awaiting Review", "PR Review"] }. The
grouping function reads this map before falling back to the default.

Part 4 — Performance
4.1 Debounced search
The filteredGroups memo in App.tsx runs on every keystroke scanning all
items. For large boards (100+ items), this is wasteful.
Fix: Debounce the search input by 150ms. Add a simple useDebounce hook (no
external dependency needed — 5 lines of code).

 4.2 Avoid config reload on cosmetic changes
SprintHubPanel calls _loadData() on every config update, including changes to
liquidGlass, theme, and colorBlind. These settings are purely cosmetic and do

not affect API calls.
Fix: In _sendConfig, compare the new config against the stored _lastConfig.
Only call _loadData() if a data-relevant field (owner, projectNumber,
ownerType, statusFieldName, refreshInterval) changed.

4.3 CODEOWNERS regex memoization
matchesCodeownersPattern compiles a RegExp on every call. For a PR with 30

changed files and a CODEOWNERS with 50 patterns, this is 1 500 regex
compilations per render.
Fix: Memoize entries.map(e => ({ ...e, re:
compilePattern(e.pattern) })) in PRFilesSection via useMemo, keyed on
codeownersEntries.

4.4 Virtualized list for large boards
For projects with 200+ items, rendering all cards simultaneously causes jank. The
content div scrolls but all DOM nodes are mounted.
Fix: Implement a simple windowed list using IntersectionObserver — render
placeholder divs of fixed height for off-screen items, replace with real cards as they
enter the viewport. No external library needed.

Part 6 — Error Handling Gaps
6.1 Inaccessible repository warning
When fetchLinkedPRsFromRepos receives a 403, it silently skips the repo. The
user never knows that data from a restricted repo is missing.
Fix: Collect skipped repos during fetch. If any were skipped, show a dismissible
warning: “Could not load data from: repo-name (permission denied).”

6.2 Partial load recovery
If pagination fails mid-load (cursor-based, 100 items per page), the whole load fails.
For boards with 200+ items, this loses all data.
Fix: Implement partial load recovery — keep the items fetched so far, show a
warning banner “Loaded 100 / 240 items — refresh to retry.”

 6.3 Stale detail panel on external merge
If the user is viewing a PR detail panel and that PR merges externally, the panel
continues to show OPEN. The state is stale.
Fix: On every data board refresh, find the currently open detailItem by id and
replace it with the updated payload version. This is a one-line change in the data
message handler.

Part 7 — UI / Visual Overhaul
Design-level improvements identified in the first round of user testing. These affect
the visual layer and the settings UX without changing data fetching logic.

7.1 Smart org and project picker in settings
Problem: The settings modal currently requires users to type the exact organization
login and project number from memory. Both values require leaving VS Code to
look up in a browser.
Solution: - On settings modal open, fire GET /user/orgs to retrieve all
organizations the authenticated user belongs to. - Render the owner field as a
combobox backed by a <datalist> populated with fetched org logins. Supports
keyboard autocomplete and manual entry. - When the owner field has a valid value
(on blur or after a 700 ms debounce), fire a GraphQL query for
organization(login).projectsV2(first: 20) (or
user(login).projectsV2) and populate a <select> dropdown for the project
number field, showing each project as #N — Title. - Fall back to the plain number
input if the fetch fails or returns an empty list.
New message types: - { type: 'fetchOrgs' } — webview → extension { type: 'fetchProjectsList'; owner: string; ownerType:
'organization' | 'user' } — webview → extension { type: 'orgsList'; logins: string[]; viewerLogin: string } —
extension → webview - { type: 'projectsList'; owner: string;
projects: Array<{ number: number; title: string }> } — extension →

webview
Additional UX: When ownerType is user, auto-populate the owner field with the
authenticated viewerLogin. Expose a theme (dark / light) toggle now that the light
theme is polished.

7.2 Liquid Glass as the sole visual mode
Problem: The UI ships two parallel style systems — a flat “default” mode and the
liquid glass overlay. This doubles CSS surface area and complicates every future
design change. The flat mode is visually less interesting and no longer the intended
experience.

 Solution: - Always apply the liquid-glass CSS class regardless of the config
setting. - Remove the Liquid Glass toggle from the settings modal. - Archive the flat
style rules (the base card/panel backgrounds) — they are superseded by the glass
layer. - Keep the sprinthub.liquidGlass config key for backwards compatibility
but ignore its value at runtime.
Impact: All new UI components and CSS additions are written only for the glass
context.

7.3 Liquid Glass light theme
Problem: The light theme exists in the codebase (body.light-theme) but is
commented out in the settings panel. When enabled manually, it renders flat
Catppuccin Latte colours without any glass effect — the two systems are not
combined.
Solution: Create a .liquid-glass.light-theme compound selector block that
overrides both the dark glass backgrounds and the flat light backgrounds:

content.text:
Here's what I found:

**Why it's slow — two culprits:**

1. **`fetchLinkedPRsFromRepos` blocks data delivery** (biggest one). After all project items load, it fires a *per-repo* paginated query fetching every open PR from each repo just to find the few that close board issues. On a board with 5 repos that have lots of PRs, that's 5+ sequential round trips before anything is posted to the UI.

2. **The main query paginates sequentially** — each 100-item page needs the previous cursor, so N pages = N round trips before step 1 even starts. Nothing to do about that, but step 1 compounds it.

**Why project changes show nothing** — in `handleSaveConfig` in App.tsx, we call `vscodeApi.postMessage({ type: 'updateConfig' })` and `setConfig(cfg)`, but we never reset `state` to `'loading'` or clear `data`. The `loading` message from the extension arrives later (via `onDidChangeConfiguration`), but because `state === 'data'` already, the handler only sets `isRefreshing: true` (small spinner on the button), leaving stale data on screen.

**Proposed fixes:**

| Fix | Approach | Impact |
|---|---|---|
| Project change loading | Reset `state → 'loading'` and clear `data` in `handleSaveConfig` when owner/project changed | Immediate visual |
| Progressive rendering | Post board data before linked PRs arrive; linked PRs update a second later | Board appears ~instantly |
| Eliminate `fetchLinkedPRsFromRepos` | Embed `closingPullRequests(first: 5)` directly on `Issue` nodes in the main GraphQL query | Removes N extra round trips |

The third fix eliminates the per-repo queries entirely — instead of "load all items, then loop repos", we get linked PR refs inline in the same paginated responses. The tradeoff is each page payload is slightly larger, but latency (round trips) is what hurts here, not payload size.

Want me to implement all three?

content.text:
## Performance Bottlenecks Report

### Initial Load & API Calls

**1. N+1 Pagination Pattern in `fetchLinkedPRsFromRepos()` (githubService.ts:407-471)**
- Fetches open PRs **sequentially per repository** using `Promise.all()` but each repo's pagination is a **do-while loop** that fetches one page at a time
- For a project with PRs across 5 repos, each with >100 open PRs, this requires 5+ sequential GraphQL calls per repo per page
- **Bottleneck**: Line 415 GraphQL call repeated in loop for each page; no batching across repos

**2. Sequential Conflict Check Triggers on Every Load (SprintHubPanel.ts:263, 392-393)**
- After project data loads, `_checkConflicts()` is called, which fetches PR files for ALL open PRs
- In `fetchAllOpenPRFiles()` (githubService.ts:750), capped at 15 PRs in parallel, then waits for all to complete before returning
- For a board with 30+ open PRs, this is 2 API batches minimum
- **Bottleneck**: REST calls to `/pulls/{number}/files` per PR (line 753) happen after main project load completes

**3. Linked PR Check Runs — N+1 Pattern (githubService.ts:674-702)**
- `fetchLinkedPRChecks()` merges closing PRs + cross-references, then fetches check-runs **per PR** via REST
- Line 678: `fetchCheckRunsForCommit()` is called in `Promise.all()` but each requires a separate REST request
- For 10 linked PRs = 10 REST calls in parallel, each hitting `/commits/{sha}/check-runs`
- **Bottleneck**: No batching; could use GitHub's check-runs GraphQL field if available

**4. Per-Item Body Fetch on Demand (githubService.ts:1029-1044)**
- Item bodies are **explicitly excluded from bulk query** (line 80 comment)
- Each open card triggers a separate GraphQL call when clicked
- **Bottleneck**: Line 1036 GraphQL call per item; no caching between views

**5. CodeOwners File — Sequential Attempts (githubService.ts:997-1012)**
- Three `tryPath()` await calls in series (lines 1010-1012)
- **Bottleneck**: Could parallelize all three paths with `Promise.all()`

**6. Settings Queries — Separate Calls (githubService.ts:1048-1094)**
- `fetchSettingsOwners()` (line 1050+) and `fetchSettingsProjects()` (line 1068+) are called independently from SprintHubPanel
- **Bottleneck**: No caching; if settings UI loads both, two separate GraphQL requests fire

---

### Summary Table

| Bottleneck | File:Line | Impact |
|------------|-----------|--------|
| Pagination loop per repo | githubService.ts:415 | 5-10 extra calls per project load |
| Sequential conflict PR fetch | SprintHubPanel.ts:393 | 15-30 REST calls after main load |
| Check-runs N+1 (no batching) | githubService.ts:678 | 1 call per linked PR |
| Body fetch uncached per view | githubService.ts:1036 | 1 call per card open |
| CodeOwners sequential paths | githubService.ts:1010-1012 | 2 extra calls if not found first |
| Standalone settings queries | githubService.ts:1050, 1068 | 2 calls instead of 1 combined |

Here's what's making it slow, in order of impact:

**Biggest culprits:**

1. **Conflict check blocks the initial paint** — after all project data loads, `_checkConflicts()` fires synchronously and fetches PR files for every open PR (up to 15 at a time via REST). With 30+ open PRs that's 2+ full batches before the board appears. This is the most impactful fix: fire it in the background after the board renders.

2. **Linked PR check-runs are N REST calls** — one `/commits/{sha}/check-runs` request per linked PR, called after the main data arrives. With 10 linked PRs, that's 10 more serial-ish requests.

3. **Pagination loops are sequential per repo** — each repo's PR pages are fetched one at a time in a `do-while` loop.

4. **CodeOwners fetches 3 paths sequentially** — three `await tryPath()` calls that could be one `Promise.all`.

The other wins (#2–4) are smaller but addable on top.

FILE: src/SprintHubPanel.ts:46
BODY: The cache key is global, so cached board data will be reused across different `owner` / `projectNumber` / `ownerType` / `statusFieldName` values. If a user changes settings (or has multiple workspaces/projects), they can briefly see the wrong project’s board until the refresh completes. Consider scoping the cache key to the current config (e.g., include owner/projectNumber/ownerType/statusFieldName) or storing metadata alongside the cached payload and validating it before using the cache.

---
FILE: src/SprintHubPanel.ts:283
BODY: `_checkConflicts(data)` is now started before linked PR enrichment completes, but `_checkConflicts` explicitly includes `data.linkedIssuePRs` when building the PR list. Since `fetchProjectData` currently returns `linkedIssuePRs: []`, this background conflict scan will miss conflicts from linked PRs (regression vs when linked PRs were part of the initial payload). Consider either (1) awaiting linked PR fetch and passing an enriched `RunwayData` into `_checkConflicts`, or (2) re-running `_checkConflicts` once `linkedIssuePRs` arrive.

---
FILE: src/SprintHubPanel.ts:278
BODY: `globalState.update(...)` returns a Thenable that can reject (e.g., storage/quota issues). Using `void` here drops any rejection and can lead to unhandled promise rejections or silent cache write failures. Consider awaiting it inside the `try` (or attaching a `.catch(...)` that logs) so cache write failures are handled explicitly.

---
FILE: src/githubService.ts:570
BODY: `onPage?.(buildRunwayData(allNodes, ...))` rebuilds and re-parses the entire accumulated dataset on every paginated fetch. For large projects this becomes progressively more expensive (work grows with each page) and can offset the perceived loading gains. Consider maintaining incremental `groups`/`sprintsSet` state across pages (and only appending the new nodes), or having `onPage` accept a delta + metadata instead of rebuilding from scratch each time.
---
FILE: webview-ui/App.tsx:220
BODY: Progressive `data` messages mean this sprint-filter validation/auto-select runs on partial payloads. Because the one-time auto-select is finalized on the first `data` message, if the first page doesn’t include the newest sprint, the UI can auto-select the wrong sprint and never correct it as more pages arrive. Consider deferring auto-select until `dataComplete`, or updating the auto-selected sprint until the full dataset is known.
---
FILE: src/SprintHubPanel.ts:258
BODY: When cached data is present, it’s posted to the webview but `_updateStatusBar(cached)` isn’t called. This means the status bar blocker watchdog (and `showBlockers` quick-pick data) won’t be available until the first network page arrives, even though the board is already visible from cache. Consider updating the status bar from `cached` as well so offline/slow-start scenarios still show blocker status immediately.

## Summary: Key CSS/Visual Patterns for Liquid Glass & Glass Refraction

### 1. **FlyonUI Blog** (Tailwind CSS Approach)
- **Backdrop**: `backdrop-blur-lg`, `backdrop-blur-[1px]` for frosted effect
- **Opacity layers**: `bg-white/10`, `border border-white/20` for translucence
- **Depth**: Subtle `shadow-lg` for floating appearance
- **SVG filters**: `feTurbulence` + `feDisplacementMap` for rippled/frosted distortion
- **Animation**: `@keyframes` shifting `background-position` over 15s loops for organic motion

### 2. **henryoman/Water** (Utility-First Library)
- **Core glass**: `backdrop-filter` + blur + edge sheen via `.glass` class
- **Depth simulation**: Dual-tone gradients + rim effects (no blur needed)
- **Border dimension**: Razor rims + inner shadow glow
- **CSS custom properties**: `--glass-*`, `--widget-*` tokens for reusable configuration
- **Lightweight**: 3 kB minified; pure CSS, no JavaScript

### 3. **Z1Code/glass-refraction** (Advanced Refraction)
- **Backdrop base**: `backdrop-filter` with `--gr-blur: 26px` (CSS variable)
- **Refraction**: SVG `feTurbulence` + `feDisplacementMap` with configurable scales (8, 16)
- **Gradients**: RGBA backgrounds (dark, transparent transitions) for depth
- **Chromatic dispersion**: Colored overlay layers using `--gr-chromatic-blue/pink/violet` with staggered opacity
- **Specular highlights**: Animated breathing highlights + top-edge specular line (5s `--gr-specular-duration`)
- **Hierarchy**: `--gr-radius` and `--gr-saturation` (1.7→1.3) adjustments per tier

**Most actionable patterns**: Combine `backdrop-filter` blur with low-opacity borders, layer gradients for depth, use SVG displacement mapping for refraction, and animate specular highlights for polish.

Clean. Here's what the full fix does:

**Extension side** (`SprintHubPanel.ts`):
- `_fetchLinkedPRsBackground` now builds a `_linkedByIssue` map (issue number → linked PR board items) after the background fetch completes
- `_fetchLinkedPRs` still tries `fetchLinkedPRChecks` first, but if it returns empty (whether due to rate limits, timeout, or genuinely no results), it falls back to `_linkedByIssue`

**Webview side** (`App.tsx`):
- `detailItemRef` tracks the currently open detail item without stale closure issues
- When `linkedIssuePRs` arrives, if a detail panel is open for an issue that now has board-level linked PRs, it updates `linkedPRs` — covering the race where the user opened the panel before the background fetch finished

**`githubService.ts`**: Linked PR board items now carry `closingIssueNumbers` so the reverse lookup works.
